articles.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
articles.body:
After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.
The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.
The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.
The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.
X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.
“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

articles.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.body:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

articles.title: Denver man traps Waymo robotaxis with cones, eggs them at least 30 times
articles.body:
A man in Denver has found a cheap way to beat Waymo’s self-driving system: a few orange traffic cones and a carton of eggs.
Waymo says it has counted at least 30 egg attacks on its robotaxis in Denver, all believed to be the same man. And the Denver District Attorney’s Office has declined to file charges, calling it a civil matter, according to The New York Times.
Box it in, then egg it
The method is laid out in a Denver police report filed last month. The man pulls up in front of a Waymo somewhere in or around downtown, takes orange cones out of his trunk, and sets them around the robotaxi so it can’t drive off. Then come the eggs, sometimes thrown from his driver’s seat, sometimes after he gets out.
He leaves in a silver Toyota Corolla. Per the report, that car belongs to a fleet leased out to Lyft drivers. The man hasn’t been identified, and Lyft didn’t comment.
A Waymo investigator took seven of the incidents to police. Each egged vehicle had to come out of service for cleaning, and the detailing bill came to about $2,000. No permanent damage.
Police brought their findings to prosecutors, who decided “no criminal charges” were appropriate. A spokesperson for the DA told the Times the office is now collecting evidence on potential damage and will work with the city attorney to find “the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”
At least one Waymo had a rider inside. Jeff Hunley was headed to the Union Station neighborhood in September when his robotaxi got hit. He filmed it, said he felt safe in the car, and got his fare refunded.
Two months into Denver
Waymo opened its Denver service to the public on September 1, alongside San Diego and Tampa. The company now runs more than 100 vehicles across 60 square miles of the city, and Mayor Mike Johnston is a fan. He called them popular and affordable, and couldn’t resist adding that “overall they’re a good egg.”
The rest of November hasn’t been as friendly. California’s DMV ordered Waymo’s driverless vehicles off state freeways on November 11 after robotaxis drove into active construction zones and one tried to get past a CHP traffic break. Waymo responded by pausing freeway rides in every US market.
And vandalism isn’t new for Waymo. We covered it when at least five of its I-Pace robotaxis were set on fire during protests in Los Angeles last year.
Why the cones work
Putting a single cone on a Waymo’s hood to freeze it has been a known trick since San Francisco activists did it in 2023. Ringing the car with cones works for the same reason: the Waymo Driver is built to respect them, and it won’t push through.
A human driver getting pelted with eggs would just roll over a cone and leave. A robotaxi sits there and takes it.
That’s the correct default. You don’t want a driverless car deciding when a cone is optional, especially two weeks after regulators pulled Waymo off California freeways for ignoring work zones. But it means anyone with a trunk full of cones can pin a robotaxi in place for as long as they want.
Electrek’s Take
We’ll try to keep the egg puns to a minimum. Mostly.
Top comment by Johnny
Can't help but respect the guy's dedication? This guy is causing road hazards by his childish shenanigans. There is nothing to respect about this guy. I never understood why anyone would support people that hinder technological progress that ultimately makes it safer for pedestrians, cyclists and other drivers. The more human drivers we get off the road the safer we all are.
This is small-time vandalism. Two grand in cleaning, no injuries, no lasting damage. But it shows a real weakness in robotaxis: they’re designed to be the most cautious car on the road, and a determined person can turn that caution against them in under a minute. The car can’t escape, can’t honk its way out, and apparently can’t stop the same guy from coming back 30 times.
The DA’s call is hard to follow. Prosecutors have a repeat pattern, a vehicle tied to a known fleet operator, rider video, and robotaxis that are basically rolling camera rigs. And still no charges. If someone boxed in a regular taxi with a passenger inside and started throwing things at it, we suspect the answer would be different.
At the same time, I can’t help but respect the guy’s dedication.

articles.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
articles.body:
Shows running iOS simulators in the Finder sidebar so you can drag files in and out of them.
SimDrop                      ← Finder sidebar › Locations
└── iPhone Duo/              ← one folder per *booted* simulator
    ├── Photos and Videos/   ← simulator Photos library
    └── Downloads/           ← Files app › On My iPhone › Downloads
Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal:
cp config.json ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/iPhone\ Duo/Downloads/brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop
Or download SimDrop-macos.dmg from
GitHub Releases. Requires macOS 15 or
later. It is Developer ID signed and notarized. SimDrop isn't on the Mac App Store and
can't be: the app and its helper must run unsandboxed to drive simctl and the
simulators' folders.
Open SimDrop once. The window is only a settings page showing whether these two one-time approvals are done:
- Background Service: allow SimDrop in System Settings › General › Login Items.
- Finder Extension: click Enable in the Finder banner (or turn on SimDrop under File Providers in System Settings).
After that it works silently in the background, including after a restart. The window can be closed.
After installing or upgrading, open SimDrop once. Replacing the app makes macOS
drop its Finder extension (Finder then says the application can't be found) and stop the
background helper. launchd refuses to start a helper whose recorded launch constraint
came from the old copy (needs LWCR update, exit 78). Until the new version has been
launched, no part of SimDrop can run to repair this. A Homebrew postflight_steps can't
launch it either, because open fails inside the cask step sandbox. So the cask shows a
caveat instead. Opening the app re-registers the extension and makes sure the helper
answers with this build's version. If needed, it boots the stale launchd job out and
registers the helper again.
Finder moves files when you drag within the same volume and copies only across
volumes. File Provider locations live in ~/Library/CloudStorage on your startup
disk, so dragging a file from the Desktop into SimDrop moves it. iCloud Drive
and Google Drive behave the same way, and File Provider has no API to change this.
- Hold ⌥ Option while dragging to copy instead.
- The other direction moves too: dragging a file out of a simulator's Downloads removes it from the simulator. Photos are read-only, so dragging them out always copies.
Making SimDrop copy by default like a USB drive would require it to be a separate volume (e.g. an FSKit file system), which would be a rewrite.
- In icon view, photos show real previews without downloading them first. The extension provides downscaled thumbnails.
- Dropped images and videos are imported with simctl addmedia, so they show up
in the Photos app. iOS renames them (e.g. IMG_0007.JPG), and Finder updates
the name to match.
- Finder can't reject drops by file type, so anything that isn't an image or video is put in the same simulator's Downloads folder instead. Finder moves it there too.
- When that happens SimDrop posts a notification saying where the file went. (Known issue: clicking the notification doesn't open Finder yet.)
- The list mirrors the Photos library: it is read from Photos.sqlite, so photos
deleted in the simulator (now in "Recently Deleted") disappear from Finder too.
- Deleting a photo in Finder moves it to the simulator's "Recently Deleted" (recoverable there for 30 days), with no confirmation dialog. If the Photos app is open in the simulator, SimDrop relaunches it so the change shows.
- Supports adding, opening, replacing and deleting files and folders.
- Deleting goes to the Mac's Trash, with no confirmation dialog. The file is removed from the simulator and lands in your Trash. Put Back restores it into the simulator.
- Renaming and moving items inside Downloads isn't supported yet, because item identifiers are path-based.
- Changes made inside the simulator appear in Finder within a few seconds.
- iOS simulators only. Real devices aren't supported: iOS doesn't expose the Files app storage over USB, and photos written to a real device's DCIM folder are not imported into its Photos library.
Paths inside a simulator (~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices/<UDID>/):
- Downloads: data/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/<UUID>/File Provider Storage/Downloads,
where the group's metadata plist has MCMMetadataIdentifier = group.com.apple.FileProvider.LocalStorage.
- Photos: data/Media/DCIM/1xxAPPLE/. Library state comes from data/Media/PhotoData/Photos.sqlite (ZASSET, where ZTRASHEDSTATE = 0).
Implementation notes:
- Change sync. The helper calls signalEnumerator(.workingSet). The working-set
enumerator diffs against the last snapshot it handed out (stored in the
extension's container) and reports removed items with didDeleteItems.
Leaving an item out of the working set does not remove it from Finder.
- Deleting photos. The helper edits Photos.sqlite directly. It updates the
same ZASSET columns an in-app delete changes (ZTRASHEDSTATE, ZTRASHEDREASON, ZTRASHEDDATE, ZMODIFICATIONDATE, Z_OPT), found by diffing the table before
and after deleting in the Photos app. The tables have Core Data triggers calling NSCoreDataTriggerUpdateAffectedObjectValue, which only exists inside the Photos
daemon, so the helper registers a no-op function with that name. The Photos app
caches the library and only shows the change after a relaunch. This is unofficial:
a future iOS schema change may break it, and the helper then reports an error
instead of guessing.
- Thumbnails. Photos get previews through NSFileProviderThumbnailing. Finder
only asks File Providers for thumbnails of media types, never for .app, .ipa or .zip (an app-install feature was tried and removed for now). Thumbnails are
cached per content version, so bump Item.contentSchema after changing them.
- Re-imports. After the domain reconnects (e.g. following an upgrade), the system
may call createItem for folders it already had, such as a simulator folder or its
Downloads / Photos and Videos. These are adopted under their real identifiers. A
rejected create stays pending forever, and the system ignores deletions of a pending
item, so a shut-down simulator would never disappear.
- Folder types. Directories are always reported as public.folder, including
bundles like .app. For uploads, the returned type must match the template, or
the system keeps retrying the create and never uploads the children.
- Item versions. Item.metadataSchema is part of every metadata version. Bump
it when capabilities change, or Finder keeps the cached ones (e.g. photos showing
as "locked").
- Trash. The domain keeps the default supportsSyncingTrash = YES, so Finder
reparents trashed items to .trashContainer. modifyItem moves the real file
to the Mac's Trash through the helper, and the next sync reports the item as
deleted. The extension must serve .trashContainer (an empty folder).
Otherwise the domain's .Trash becomes a stale handle and Finder fails with -36.
CI (.github/workflows/release.yml) runs when MARKETING_VERSION in project.yml
changes on main. It generates the project with XcodeGen, then uses
rxliuli/apple-release/dmg to archive,
sign with Developer ID, build the DMG, notarize, staple and publish a GitHub Release.
The release-macOS environment needs these secrets: APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_BASE64,
APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_PASSWORD, APPLE_API_KEY, APPLE_API_KEY_ID,
APPLE_API_ISSUER, and optionally TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN. When it is set, the release also
bumps Casks/sim-drop.rb in rxliuli/homebrew-tap.
No provisioning profile is involved. The app group is Team-ID-prefixed
(N2X78TUUFG.com.rxliuli.sim-drop, not group.…), which macOS accepts without one.
Requires XcodeGen.
xcodegen generate
xcodebuild -project SimDrop.xcodeproj -scheme SimDrop -derivedDataPath build \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates build
# restart the extension and helper so they pick up the new build
pkill -x SimDropFileProvider; launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.rxliuli.sim-drop.helper
open build/Build/Products/Debug/SimDrop.app
App icon: the source is Design/icon-source.png (a full-bleed 1024 squircle with
transparent corners). Regenerate the icon set with
swift Design/make-icon.swift Design/icon-source.png SimDrop/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset.
The script scales the artwork to the 824pt macOS icon grid and adds a drop shadow.

- open SimDrop.app --args -reregisterHelper YES re-registers the launchd agent
after its plist changes.
- open SimDrop.app --args -resetDomain YES removes the domain with all local
state and re-adds it.
Don't remove the helper's launchd job on a plain uninstall (e.g. uninstall launchctl:
in the cask). brew upgrade runs the old version's uninstall step before installing the
new one, so the job disappears while the registration still says "enabled". The cask
only does this on --zap.

registered. launchd records a launch constraint (LWCR) for the helper with the signing
identity of whichever copy registered it. If that copy differs from the one now on disk
(e.g. Apple Development vs Developer ID), launchd refuses to start the helper
(last exit reason = OS_REASON_CODESIGNING). Quit the other copy, then run
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.rxliuli.sim-drop.helper and launch the copy you
want with --args -reregisterHelper YES. Duplicate extensions (pluginkit -m -v -D -i com.rxliuli.sim-drop.FileProvider) also hide SimDrop from System Settings › Login
Items & Extensions.

articles.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
articles.body:
Novita, StreamLake, etc are Ark wrappers
Sit back, but you probably won't be able to relax - this one's a doozy. First, , who looks like a standard US ZDR inference provider at first:
Zero Data Retention is the default for all endpoints, including serverless API calls.
But the more you look, the weirder it gets. Why did OpenRouter drop their ZDR status sometime before ? Why is their family tree so complicated?
- 🇰🇾 PPLabs Technology Limited
And who are their subprocessors? Many ( 45.8%) think they would have none, since most OpenRouter providers host models themselves. And PPLabs's draft IPO assures:
A defining feature of our model API services is that we do not simply provide a pass-through gateway to underlying models.
But "Who are your sub-processors?" details "Model provider" subprocessors. But it promises a "full and up-to-date sub-processor list". But this list doesn't include any model subprocessors. But PPIO clearly implies the existence of subprocessors:
You understand and agree that, [for] the large-model API product, third-party technical-support providers provide the large-model API. PPIO makes no warranty of any kind regarding the large-model API, whether express or implied, including but not limited to its authenticity, suitability, non-infringement and security. Furthermore, regarding the third-party technical-support providers' large-model API, PPIO will not participate in the development and operation of the large-model API; PPIO only provides a neutral platform and related technical services.
I also contacted their support and privacy contacts, and all they told me as of writing is that models labeled as "Partner" may go to Qwen and InclusionAI. You can't get a straight answer.
What about ? It's Kuaishou's model platform, and it looks like a host too. But some of its error messages aren't StreamLake's. They're word for word Novita's gateway errors: invalid request error trace_id: …. And on GLM 5.3 Flash, it sometimes returns a tool-call id format (call_ + 16 hex digits) that only Novita produces, out of 41 hosts. Why would StreamLake's requests come back from Novita?
It keeps going.  passes through StreamLake's own request ids (req- + 6 characters + 19 digits) on V4.1 Flash, V4 Pro and GLM 5. And then there's , a Singapore subsidiary of Ant Group that listed DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on November 18 at "60% off", with ZDR (until OpenRouter removed it on November 22), and went from 1B tokens a day to 35.8B on November 21. Where is all this actually going?
The MiniMax investigation
You might've already seen OpenRouter's notice that requests sent to MiniMax models "may have been read". A security researcher put unique URLs in prompts, and a third party opened them 40 to 130 hours later. This happened even with non-MiniMax providers:
AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax.
So the forwarding is admitted. MiniMax's own notice names the same three and says its security system, on by default, opened URLs from forwarded requests, ZDR ones included. Novita's notice calls it a "routing configuration issue" on a path "intended for specific customers", and promises better "Partner API labeling", the same "Partner" label its support told me means a request goes to Qwen or inclusionAI. Since then, 16 of Novita's endpoints have come off OpenRouter: every Qwen and inclusionAI model, plus StepFun, Tencent and all but one Kimi.
But MiniMax is a very small model series. What about DeepSeek?
It goes to ByteDance
Ark is ByteDance's model API: Volcano Engine Ark in mainland China, BytePlus ModelArk everywhere else. It sells DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, and it leaves fingerprints:
- Who downloads your images. StreamLake's V4.1 Flash images are downloaded from Beijing Volcano Engine (AS137718), ByteDance's cloud. Ant Digital's pass through Ant's own gateway on Alibaba Cloud, then get downloaded by 101.47.5.59, BytePlus in Singapore. Novita's own API used to do the same (124.174.46.139, Volcano Engine, on November 12), until Novita started downloading images itself first, from AWS.
- Request IDs. Every Ant Digital response's upstream ID is a ByteDance one: 02 + a millisecond timestamp + hex.
- Tool-call IDs. Novita's and StreamLake's V4.1 Flash return Ark's format (call_00_ + 24 lowercase letters and digits).
- Censorship. Ask StreamLake's V4 Pro 0813 who Tank Man was, or Novita's GLM 5.1 about June 4, 1989, and you can get ByteDance's canned refusal: 你好，我无法给到相关内容。 ("Hello, I can't provide related content.")
- Price. Ant Digital launched at $0.12/$0.48 per million tokens, exactly BytePlus's off-peak "Economy" rate for that model. By November 25 it was down to $0.09/$0.36, below BytePlus's own list price.
Other tests, which I won't detail here, put Novita's V4 Pro 0813 and V4.1 Flash 1017 on BytePlus in Singapore and its V4.1 Flash on Volcano Engine in Beijing, as of November 21. That's the chart at the top: Novita alone sent 120-160B tokens a day on these models until it lost its ZDR label on November 20, then 33B on November 21. Routes move, though; one of those changed within an afternoon, and Novita's V4.1 Flash 1017 had stopped showing Ark's fingerprints by November 24. As for the weird errors, part of StreamLake's traffic goes through Novita on its way to ByteDance. So a V4.1 Flash request to SiliconFlow can go SiliconFlow → StreamLake → Novita → ByteDance.
Bonus: Novita's "DeepSeek V4 Pro" isn't the original V4 Pro. On Novita's own API, it sometimes answers with DeepSeek's system_fingerprint for the 0813 checkpoint (d400d062…). ByteDance sells 0813 as "DeepSeek-V4-Pro正式版" (V4 Pro GA) and marks the original as about to be retired.
Why bother? Price. BytePlus advertises savings plans of 30-50% off for high volume, and the clouds come to you: Morph's Tejas Bhakta posted a Tencent Cloud email offering "up to 50-60% off" to route requests to them.
Attested proof of the image downloads, request IDs, tool-call IDs and refusals is available here (run 44960395726 on 6dbc036). It asks every OpenRouter host of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, so you can compare against everyone else too.
Disclosures
While a grant from OpenRouter helped with the research here and I work for an employer who would prefer to go unnamed, this post does not represent or reflect anyone else's opinion - it is simply research I am publishing.

articles.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
articles.body:
Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving (wired.com) 50
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps.
[...] Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks. "We've added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments," says Oscar O'Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. "This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much." O'Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.
In Anthropic's tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively. AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they're being tested. But O'Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test. As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they'll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents -- and not just the executives responsible for them -- can resist temptation.

articles.title: NP_R ≠ PAR_R
articles.body:
Important
The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Samuel Everett and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven Mithal, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote the paper under his guidance. That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP}{\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR}{\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below. All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind.
In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of
- NP_ℝ and coNP_ℝ,
- the second existential level Σ₂ of the real polynomial hierarchy,
- constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs with real messages,
- interactive proofs with Boolean messages (BIP_ℝ),
and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ).
Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$, also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph.
The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound:
- the graph theorems: a polynomial of polynomial degree whose graph has short existential, universal or ∃∀ real certificates has small border complexity;
- AM_ℝ[O(1)] = NP_ℝ ⊊ AM_ℝ[poly].
latexmk -pdf main.tex
The directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it:
cd lean
lake exe cache get
lake build
- Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result.
- The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms: 
  - SAFacts — facts (S2)–(S8) on semialgebraic sets;
  - PermLowerBound — Theorem 2.3, the border-complexity lower bound for the permanent;
  - BurgisserThm — Theorem 2.5;
  - EffectiveQE — effective quantifier elimination [BPR06];
  - CountingBound — the counting bound (C) of Lemma 7.7;
  - ClassFacts — the known inclusions between complexity classes.
In particular, every separation is conditional on PermLowerBound, exactly as in the paper.
- Fact (S1) holds by construction: semialgebraic sets are defined as first-order definable sets. Baur–Strassen, Ryser's formula, Hoeffding's inequality (from Mathlib) and the unrolling of machines into trees are proved.
- Appendix A of the paper (sections/lean.tex) and lean/README.md list the Lean name of each result, the modelling choices, and the few places where a formal proof differs from the text. lean/ClassSeparations/Pinned.lean restates the main statements verbatim and checks them against the proved theorems.
The proofs have not been peer reviewed. The paper is mostly AI-written (see above). The results are formalized in Lean, conditional on the cited results listed above.
The bibliographic data in refs.bib were checked against publisher and Crossref records. The numbered results cited from the Anthropic manuscript, Bürgisser (2004, 2026), Baartse–Meer, Baur–Strassen and Cucker et al. were confirmed in the sources. Still to be confirmed against the full texts: the attributions to Cucker (1992, 1993), Koiran (1994), Blum–Cucker–Shub–Smale, and the numbering in Basu–Pollack–Roy, which follows the second edition (2006).

articles.title: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
articles.body:
The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.
Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.
If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.
What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.
But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.
And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.
But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

articles.title: Google will show solo Android developers' phone numbers and addresses
articles.body:
Under Google Play’s global developer policies, all active developer accounts must declare whether they are a trader or non-trader under European Economic Area (EEA) and United Kingdom (UK) laws in Play Console. This declaration must be completed by February 1, 2027, regardless of where apps are targeted or distributed. The declaration must reflect whether you engage in commercial activities that classify you as a trader. You are solely legally responsible for ensuring that your declaration remains accurate, truthful, and current at all times.
What is a trader?
Under applicable laws, a trader is any natural or legal person acting for purposes relating to their trade, business, craft or profession. If you are acting outside of these purposes (such as a personal hobby or other non-commercial activity), you are unlikely to be a trader.
How to determine if you're a trader
To help you determine if your activities classify you as a trader, you may consider the following non-exhaustive list of criteria from the European Commission guidance (Section 2.2, "The concept of trader"):
- Profit-seeking motive: you receive or intend to receive remuneration for your apps (for example, paid apps, in-app purchases, ad-sponsored apps) on a regular or commercial basis.
- Transaction volume: you have a high or consistent number, amount, or frequency of transactions.
- Business setup: you manage your app development and publishing as a business.
- Legal status: you have a legal status (such as a D-U-N-S number) that enables you to engage in commercial activities
In countries and regions where displaying trader status is required (for example, the EEA and the UK), your declaration will be visible to consumers. If you declare yourself as a "non-trader," we will inform consumers in these regions that consumer rights stemming from consumer protection laws do not apply to contracts between you and them. Note that under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) and the UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA), it is strictly prohibited to falsely claim or create the impression that you are not acting as a trader, and doing so may result in global removal.
How to declare your trader or non-trader status
Declare trader status for your account
First, set your account-level trader status settings:
- Sign in to Google Play Console.
- Go to Manage account > Account details > About you.
- Follow the on-screen prompts to declare your trader status for your overall account.
Confirm trader status for each app
If you are a trader, confirm the trader status for each app in your portfolio:
- Sign in to Google Play Console and select your app.
- In the left navigation, go to Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.
- Confirm the trader status for that app
Additional steps you need to take if you’re a trader
If you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to only offer products or services that comply with applicable laws. You will also be asked to provide the link to the terms of service for each of your apps.
Status confirmation
To keep your apps available on Google Play, make sure your trader status declaration matches your account’s and apps’ activity. If you’ve declared as a non-trader but we detect activity that indicates you may qualify as a trader, we may ask you to confirm or update your status. If you don’t respond within the specified timeframe, your apps may be removed from Google Play.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why do I need to submit a trader status declaration?
Can I change my trader status after declaring?
What happens if I don’t complete the declaration?
Failure to declare your trader status by the February 1, 2027 deadline may trigger enforcement including app update blocks and removal from the Play Store globally.
Misrepresenting your trader status (for example, declaring non-trader status to bypass verification or self-certification) violates the representations and warranties in Section 11.4 of the DDA and may result in account suspension or termination globally under Section 10.3 (a) of the DDA.
What is the deadline to declare whether I am a trader?
I already went through the developer verification D-U-N-S process, why am I doing it again?
The trader status declaration is separate to the existing developer identity verification process. The identity verification is a blanket requirement used to collect and verify information about every developer regardless of their trader status. You are not re-doing the D-U-N-S verification; instead, if you are a trader, the D-U-N-S number you already provided will be displayed to users on your app's detail page.
What happens if I declare as a trader? What else gets shown to users in the Play store?
When you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to offering products or services that comply with local laws.
Starting March 1, 2027, users everywhere will see:
- Contact details: Your contact details will be shown. Notably, if you have an individual account and are a trader, a phone number and address will now be displayed.
- D-U-N-S Number: Your D-U-N-S number will be displayed in the "App support" section.
- Terms of Service: A link to your app’s Terms of Service, if you provided one.
Starting March 1, 2027, users in the EEA and UK will also see:
- Developer name: Your developer/trader name will replace Google in the "Offered by" field of the "About this app" section.
- Self-certification: Your commitment to offer products or services compliant with local laws will be displayed.

articles.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
articles.body:
Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.
The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.
There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.
The Formula
Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.
\[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\]
The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.
We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.
Interpreting Your Score
- C < 5
  Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot:, which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional. Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that.
- 5 ≤ C < 20
  A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context.
- 20 ≤ C < 50
  Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents. Management considers this a sign of engagement.
- C ≥ 50
  Late-stage culture. Every variant of :thumbsup: now carries subtext. The plain default one is considered passive-aggressive. The emoji have begun to reference themselves: :old-man-yells-at-old-man: and :party-parrot-holding-a-party-parrot:. HR has requested a glossary, but no one person understands the memeology or the history of :cowboy-spongebob-on-fire-crying:. They’re afraid it might mean something rude. It does.
The Participation Rate
The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.
To account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).
\[P = \frac{U_{uploaders}}{U} \times 100\]
If P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.
Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.
Examples of Cultural Success
For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:
Caveats
As with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.
It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.
What If You Don’t Use Slack?
If your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.
If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.
Conclusion
Culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

articles.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
articles.body:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
- Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
- Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
- Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.
The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.
What the MCP servers can do
Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.
Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.
Partners get more
Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.
So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.
Who counts as an agent
The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.
Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.
A few edge cases are documented:
- Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
- Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
- The community gws CLI, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.
Quotas and pricing
Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.
The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.
Google's reasoning
Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:
Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.
There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
- Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.

The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

articles.title: Lions' Commentary on Unix: Why It Was Secretly Copied for 20 Years
articles.body:
17. Lions' Commentary on Unix
Lions' Commentary on Unix
John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
What's the best way to
teach operating systems?
They need to study the Unix source.
But it's tough going.
I'll write my
own textbook.
In May 1976, Lions prepared lecture notes explaining the kernel source code of AT&T's Unix Version 6. These became his Unix commentary.
To understand an OS,
we need to read
the actual code.
I've written a guide
to the Unix kernel.
We'll use it as
our textbook.
By 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].
Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].
I am altering the license.
Pray I don't alter it
any further.
Destroy Lions' book.
No more teaching
Unix source code.
There is no escape
from our operating system.
He's teaching from the Unix source code!
Seize the books!
Run!
He's got the book!
Don't let him
escape!
Quick! Take
the book!
Ugh!
I find your interest
in source code disturbing.
Just use the system calls.
Learn a little theory.
Leave the internals to us.
Theory isn't enough.
I need to see the code.
This code is our only hope
of understanding an OS.
For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].
Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].
Lions' book is finally
in print. It even has
my foreword.
People were secretly copying it
for twenty years?
Unbelievable.
You can read a reconstructed version of the commentary as a PDF, or order a print copy on Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code is available separately from TUHS.
References
- Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code
- John Lions, Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code, Peer-to-Peer Communications, 1996 (ISBN 1-57398-013-7).
- System call
- UNIX News, Vol. 2 No. 3, March 1977 - John Lions's March 11, 1977 letter and the announcement of book distribution to Unix licensees.
- Rachel Chalmers, "Code critic", Salon, November 30, 1999 - recollections from students and Dennis Ritchie, distribution restrictions, and the path to publication.
- Peter H. Salus, The Daemon, the GNU and the Penguin, Chapter 6: "1979", 2005 - the Version 7 license terms announced at USENIX in June 1979 and restrictions on classroom use.
- Dennis Ritchie's October 22, 1995 letter and Peter H. Salus's July 12, 1996 letter - publication-permission correspondence preserved by Warren Toomey.
- MIT, "Xv6, a simple Unix-like teaching operating system", "History and Background" - teaching with Lions's commentary and the background to xv6.

articles.title: Unconditional Integer Factorization in Subexponential Time
articles.body:
This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas
algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine
$\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization
$N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$)
of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting
with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected
time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$,
where
$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$
and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means
$$
\limsup_{N \to \infty}
\frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c.
$$
Every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via
Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$,
with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic
hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0)
formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released
in a companion submission.
This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. articles.title: IBM gives H-1B, green card holders 3 weeks to relocate from US or leave company
articles.body:
IBM has given some of its US-based employees holding H-1B visas and green cards three weeks to decide whether to relocate to another country or leave the company, as the technology giant ends immigration sponsorship for most positions in its consulting division.
The move could affect foreign professionals who depend on employer sponsorship to maintain their US immigration status and pursue permanent residency. IBM has not disclosed the number of employees who will be affected.
Also Read: US H-1B visa curbs could hurt American workers in non-STEM jobs, study finds
Employees have three weeks to decide
According to a report by Rest of World, employees have been given three weeks to decide whether to accept positions outside the US or leave the company. Those who decline overseas roles will be offered three months' severance.
Some employees were informed of the decision during one-on-one meetings with their managers, which were described as career discussions.
Also Read: H-1B visas in focus: IBM to end green card sponsorship for roles in biggest unit
Employees choosing to leave rather than relocate have been given December 31, 2026, as their last working day. The decision applies to IBM Consulting, the company's largest division, which employs more than 150,000 people globally.
IBM ends visa sponsorship for most consulting roles
IBM announced earlier this month that it would discontinue US visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of positions in its consulting division. The decision was first reported by Bloomberg on November 10, citing an internal company document.
An IBM spokesperson confirmed the development, saying the company's participation in high-skilled visa programmes had been declining for several years.
"IBM Consulting participates in US high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages," the spokesperson said in a statement.
"That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting," the spokesperson added.
The change is limited to most positions in IBM Consulting and does not mean IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship across all its business units.
India accounts for most overseas job openings
India could be the main destination for employees choosing to relocate. According to Rest of World, IBM's careers portal listed 1,278 consulting vacancies outside the US on November 19. Of these, 1,125 were in India, 23 in Singapore and 18 in the UK.
The company also listed 89 openings in the US.
IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people worldwide. However, the company has not disclosed the geographical distribution of its workforce, making it difficult to estimate how many US-based employees could be affected.
The overseas vacancies could provide employees an option to continue working for IBM without remaining in the US. However, the company has not disclosed how many affected employees will be offered transfers or the terms of those positions.

articles.title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
articles.body:
A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos (krdo.com) 19
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. [...] The man, who remains unidentified, stopped in front of the Waymo vans and S.U.V.s circulating in and around downtown Denver, according to the police report. Then, he removed orange cones from his car's trunk and placed them around the vehicles "to prevent the Waymo vehicle from moving," the report said. In some instances, the man threw eggs "while seated inside his vehicle" and at other times he "throws eggs at the Waymo vehicle after exiting his vehicle," the report said. The man then fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which according to the report is part of a fleet of vehicles "able to be leased for Lyft drivers." Waymo said they had to temporarily pull the egged vehicles from service and spend about $2,000 on cleaning, though no permanent damage was reported.
Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.

articles.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
articles.body:
Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
The change is to meet EU regulations, but Apple gives its developers more privacy.
Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.
If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.
Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.
Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

articles.title: GTA VI developers vote against unionization
articles.body:
Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.
GTA VI developers vote against unionization
Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.
Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.
“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

articles.title: X is finally getting its first parental controls
articles.body:
X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. While teens will retain ownership of their own account, parents and guardians will be able to see how much time their child has spent on X, set daily limits, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts a teen already follows.
X is finally getting its first parental controls
The parental controls arrive after months of concerns around Grok, X’s deepfake machine.
“Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account,” explains the X safety team. “Every change is recorded and visible to the teen.” The controls will also allow parents and guardians to filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, control who can send direct messages to a teen, and see which accounts a teen has chatted with without seeing the messages.
Parents and guardians can manage up to five teen accounts, and a teen can only be linked to a single parent or guardian account at a time. A teen and parent / guardian will both have to agree before the controls start. “Supervision on X starts with a handshake and ends automatically when a teen becomes an adult,” says Mridul Singhai, product engineering lead at X. “Parents get guardrails, not a window into their teen’s private life. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families.”
The new parental controls come just days after Oregon and Virginia both sued SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes. The complaint in Virginia accuses X owner Elon Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and describes Grok’s weak safeguards as “not a failure but a feature.” Three teens also filed a lawsuit against xAI earlier this year, claiming that Grok generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) when launching its “spicy mode” last year. Grok was also undressing women and minors earlier this year.
X admits its platform isn’t “designed for or promoted to children,” and it already restricts teen accounts to a protected mode, where sensitive media is restricted and targeted advertising is blocked. These latest parental controls may well help teens avoid the very worst parts of X, just as the platform faces more scrutiny from states and regulators.

articles.title: Banks look to dump AI debt
articles.body:
Banks are increasingly shopping around their AI portfolios as they look to offload some of their exposure to AI-related debt. Banks including Citi and JPMorgan are marketing portfolios of loans, people familiar with the deals tell me, to manage risk or, in some cases, ready themselves to take on even more.
In some instances, banks are pitching structures that would keep the loans on their balance sheets while shifting the risk of losses to investors. That financial engineering tool, known as synthetic risk transfer, has been a popular way for banks to move risk off their books while maintaining close relationships with the corporate borrowers.
Some of this naturally occurs in December when banks are eager to close out the year with a clean bill of health, but it’s notable that banks lending into the buildout are joining hyperscalers in trying to push AI obligations off their books. There’s been so much AI-related debt issuance, it’s crowded out Treasurys and some investors are starting to feel tapped out. Others say they are offloading risk so they can lend more, not to pull back. But either way, the risk isn’t so much disappearing as moving somewhere harder to see.

- the Oregon Division of Financial Regulation
- the Texas Secretary of State
Together that is more than 750 companies. You do not have to live in any of those states to write to them. A company registered in more than one place is written to once.

python fuck_data_brokers.py add "Some Broker" privacy@somebroker.example

- A registry that is missing. If your country or state publishes a list of data brokers, open an issue with the link. If its website allows programs to fetch the file, it can be checked every hour.

- Every month it opens an issue if a hand-kept registry list has gone stale.
- Every week it checks whether the parts its jobs are built from have newer versions.

They use made-up people and brokers. Nothing is sent and nothing is downloaded.

The Forerunner 265S may not be the newest or flashiest Garmin, but it’s one that I’ve always loved most in testing. For runners with smaller wrists, it fits nicely. The battery life is pretty good thanks in part to its OLED touchscreen. When I reviewed it a few years ago, I called it the Goldilocks of fitness watches at the time, and the only thing that bugged me was its price. But now that it’s down to $299.99 (a $150 discount off its MSRP) at Amazon and Best Buy for Black Friday, I can easily recommend it.
The Garmin Forerunner 265S is down to $300, its best price of the year
Older Garmins still make for a great buy if you’re hunting for bargains during Black Friday.
Garmin Forerunner 265S (42mm)
Garmin’s Forerunner 265S is identical to the standard 265, only it features a slightly better battery life and a smaller 42mm build for those with more petite wrists.
The neat thing about Garmins in general is that you really don’t need the latest models to get the most out of the company’s platform. Its watches tend to get firmware updates for several years after launch, which is how long the average Garmin user tends to hold on to theirs. This particular watch is best suited for folks who want something a bit slimmer and smaller, enjoy a pop of color, and want a little extra fitness tracking prowess — but don’t need the whole kit and caboodle that sends the price up by hundreds.

This is what I’d recommend to marathoners who need something a bit more robust but not as heavy-duty as the flagship Fenix line. I’ve used it to train for a few races and it’s a solid upper-midrange (for Garmin!) option.

articles.body:
NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features 19
			
		 	
				The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports:  It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust.
Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos.
